PostgREST

Source: vignettes/postgrest.Rmd
postgrest.Rmd

PostgREST turns PostgreSQL tables and functions into an HTTP API. Read PostgreSQL tables and views through PostgREST using each visitor’s account. PostgREST validates the visitor’s JWT and PostgreSQL applies the role’s grants and row-level security policies. The R client uses HTTP and does not need RPostgres or PostgreSQL 18’s native OAuth support.

The app passes the signed-in visitor’s access token on every request. There is no separate username argument: PostgREST extracts the database role from the verified JWT’s configured role claim. A deployment can use one role per person, or a shared role with row policies that use the token’s user ID (usually sub). The role claim and the user ID are configured in the identity provider and database, so the same app query can return different rows for different logins.

Set up the server and sign-in

Configure PostgREST to trust your identity provider’s signing keys and the token audience intended for this API. Configure its JWT role extraction and allow the authenticator role to switch into the database roles you expose. Give those roles the necessary schema, table, view, and function permissions. See PostgREST’s authentication guide and database authorization guide.

Register your Shiny app with that identity provider, using http://localhost:8100 as the redirect URI for this example. Request the audience and scopes that your deployment expects. An identity token or a token intended for another API is not a substitute for this API’s access token. The example assumes the registration issues the right JWT access token through its ordinary authorization-code flow.

Set OAUTHDB_POSTGREST_ISSUER, OAUTHDB_POSTGREST_URL, OAUTHDB_CLIENT_ID, and OAUTHDB_CLIENT_SECRET in your environment. The API URL must use HTTPS; it may include a reverse proxy prefix such as /rest/v1. For a private CA, pass ca_bundle to oauth_db_postgrest_api().

For a configured local example, run shinyOAuthDB::oauth_db_demo("postgrest"). It includes PostgreSQL, PostgREST, Keycloak and an app. The local demo guide lists the accounts and cleanup command.

Setting Where to get it
OAUTHDB_POSTGREST_URL Your HTTPS PostgREST endpoint, including any proxy path such as /rest/v1
schema, table The schema exposed by PostgREST and a table the user can read
Issuer, client ID, secret The OIDC registration with the API’s trusted provider

Store the OAUTHDB_* values in .Renviron and restart R. See the server recipe after the app if your PostgreSQL database doesn’t yet expose an API.

Complete Shiny app

Replace the schema, table, and column names with your own. Save the example as example.R and run it with source("example.R").

library(shiny)
library(shinyOAuth)
library(shinyOAuthDB)

provider <- oauth_provider_oidc_discover(
  issuer = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_POSTGREST_ISSUER")
)
client <- oauth_client(
  provider,
  client_id = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_CLIENT_ID"),
  client_secret = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_CLIENT_SECRET"),
  redirect_uri = "http://localhost:8100",
  scopes = c("openid", "profile", "email", "offline_access")
)

ui <- oauth_ui(
  fluidPage(
    actionButton("login", "Sign in"),
    actionButton("logout", "Sign out"),
    tableOutput("rows")
  ),
  id = "auth",
  client = client
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  auth <- oauth_module_server("auth", client, auto_redirect = FALSE)
  observeEvent(input$login, auth$request_login())
  observeEvent(input$logout, auth$logout())

  postgrest <- oauth_db_postgrest_api(
    auth$connection,
    url = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_POSTGREST_URL"),
    schema = "reporting"
  )
  output$rows <- renderTable({
    postgrest$select("orders", order = "id.asc", limit = 20L)
  })
}

runApp(
  shinyApp(ui, server, uiPattern = ".*"),
  port = 8100,
  launch.browser = FALSE
)

# Open the app in your regular browser at http://localhost:8100
# (viewers in RStudio/Positron/etc. cannot perform necessary redirects)

Create the client inside server(). Its requests wait quietly before sign-in and use a current access token for the selected authorization. Use target if your shinyOAuth client has named token targets.

Prepare PostgreSQL, PostgREST and Keycloak

Copy a working configuration with oauth_db_demo("postgrest", action = "files"). In that directory, postgrest/fixture.sql creates an authenticator login, database roles and a row policy. realm.json adds the verified token’s role claim; PostgREST switches to that role when executing SQL.

For your deployment, create a restricted login for PostgREST and let it assume only the roles the API exposes. For example:

CREATE ROLE reporting_reader NOLOGIN;
GRANT reporting_reader TO authenticator;
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA reporting TO reporting_reader;
GRANT SELECT ON reporting.orders TO reporting_reader;

Configure the issuer’s access-token mapper to emit role=reporting_reader and the API’s audience. Set PGRST_DB_SCHEMAS to the exposed schema, PGRST_JWT_SECRET to its public JWK/JWKS material, and PGRST_JWT_AUD to that audience. The default role claim is role; configure a different claim path only if your tokens use one. Plan how to update signing keys when the provider rotates them; the demo takes a snapshot at startup. Terminate HTTPS at your API or reverse proxy.

PostgREST’s authentication guide explains key formats and role extraction. PostgreSQL table grants and row policies still control which rows the role can access.

Filters, embedded resources, and pagination

filters contains native PostgREST expressions. Values are URL-encoded; they are not SQL fragments interpolated by this package. select can include related resources configured through foreign keys.

rows <- postgrest$select(
  "orders",
  select = "id,total,customers(name)",
  filters = list(total = "gte.100", country = "eq.NL"),
  order = "id.asc",
  limit = 20L,
  offset = 20L
)
response <- postgrest$select(
  "orders",
  order = "id.asc",
  limit = 20L,
  count = "exact",
  raw = TRUE
)
httr2::resp_header(response, "Content-Range")

Selections return one page. The server can impose a smaller page size; use its Content-Range header to inspect the returned range. Exact counts can be expensive for large tables. See pagination and count.

JSON results become data frames where possible. Large integer literals remain strings; decimal precision depends on how the server serializes the value. Cast exact decimal values to text in a view or function when necessary. Embedded resources may become nested data frames or list columns. Empty selections have no column metadata and return a zero-column data frame. Dates keep their JSON representation.

Functions and native API requests

Call an exposed PostgreSQL function through its RPC endpoint. The keys in args are its argument names; the result may be a scalar, object, or table.

total <- postgrest$rpc("order_total", list(order_id = 42L))

# A GET function call runs in a read-only transaction on PostgREST.
total <- postgrest$request(
  c("rpc", "order_total"),
  query = list(order_id = 42L)
)

# Native writes use the same visitor's token and database permissions.
response <- postgrest$request(
  "orders",
  method = "PATCH",
  query = list(id = "eq.42"),
  body = list(status = "reviewed"),
  prefer = "return=representation",
  raw = TRUE
)

GET and HEAD requests retry once after HTTP 401 using a renewed token. Other methods never retry automatically: a function or write may already have changed data. Redirects are rejected. Each operation stays with the authorization that started it and discards a response if the visitor signs out, changes accounts, or loses access while it runs.
